claims.claim: In Tribolium castaneum, both pair-rule and gap genes are expressed as dynamic waves that propagate from posterior to anterior.
claims.source: In the flour beetle Tribolium castaneum, a short-germ insect thought to retain a more ancestral mode of AP patterning than long-germ insects like Drosophila, both pair-rule and gap genes are expressed as dynamic waves that propagate from posterior to anterior (El-Sherif et al., 2012a; Sarrazin et al., 2012; El-Sherif et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2017; Boos et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies on Tribolium development.

claims.claim: Pair-rule and gap genes in Drosophila undergo dynamic posterior-to-anterior shifts, though these shifts are limited compared to other insects.
claims.source: Even pair-rule and gap genes in Drosophila, classically thought to be expressed stably, were shown more recently to undergo dynamic (albeit limited) posterior-to-anterior shifts (Jaeger et al., 2004; El-Sherif and Levine, 2016; Lim et al., 2018; Berrocal et al., 2020; Keränen et al., 2006), a phenomenon that has been suggested (arguably) to be an evolutionary vestige of outright gene expression waves of the sort observed in Tribolium and other insects (Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2021; Rudolf et al., 2020; Verd et al., 2018; Clark and Peel, 2018; Clark and Desplan, 2017; Stahi and Chipman, 2016; Auman and Chipman, 2018; Xiang et al., 2017; Auman et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies that revised classical understanding of Drosophila patterning.

claims.claim: The Speed Regulation model explains the generation of periodic or non-periodic wavelike gene expression patterns.
claims.source: Some of the authors have recently suggested a model that explains the generation of either periodic or non-periodic wavelike gene expression patterns, termed the 'Speed Regulation' model (Figure 1A and B; Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2017; Boos et al., 2018; Rudolf et al., 2020; Kuhlmann and El-Sherif, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim describes a theoretical model previously proposed by some of the authors, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: In the Speed Regulation model, a morphogen gradient modulates the speed of either a molecular clock or a genetic cascade.
claims.source: In this model, a morphogen gradient (of a molecular factor termed the 'speed regulator') modulates the speed of either a molecular clock or a genetic cascade.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of the Speed Regulation model based on theoretical modeling.

claims.claim: The Speed Regulation model can produce periodic waves when modulating a molecular clock.
claims.source: This scheme was shown (in silico) to be able to produce periodic waves in the former case (Figure 1A), and non-periodic waves in the latter (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The Speed Regulation model can produce non-periodic waves when modulating a genetic cascade.
claims.source: This scheme was shown (in silico) to be able to produce periodic waves in the former case (Figure 1A), and non-periodic waves in the latter (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: A gradient of Caudal/Wnt acts as a speed regulator in generating pair-rule and gap gene expression waves in the early Tribolium embryo.
claims.source: The model was shown to be involved in generating pair-rule and gap gene expression waves in the early Tribolium embryo where a gradient of Caudal/Wnt was suggested to act as a speed regulator (El-Sherif et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by some of the authors.

claims.claim: The Enhancer Switching model posits that each patterning gene is simultaneously wired into two gene regulatory networks: a dynamic GRN and a static GRN.
claims.source: The Enhancer Switching model posits that each patterning gene is simultaneously wired into two gene regulatory networks (GRNs) (Figure 1C): (i) a dynamic GRN that drives periodic or sequential gene activities, and (ii) a static GRN that stabilizes gene expression patterns.
claims.evidence: This describes the theoretical framework of the Enhancer Switching model illustrated in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: In the Enhancer Switching model, the speed regulator activates the dynamic GRN while repressing the static GRN.
claims.source: The concentration of the speed regulator (shown in gray in Figure 1C) activates the dynamic GRN while repressing the static GRN, and hence sets the balance between the contribution of each GRN to the overall dynamics and, consequently, the speed of gene regulation (Diaz-Cuadros et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2017; Kuhlmann and El-Sherif, 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of the Enhancer Switching model, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The Enhancer Switching model proposes that each gene is regulated by two enhancers: a dynamic enhancer and a static enhancer.
claims.source: As mentioned, the model posits that each gene is wired into two different GRNs, a requirement that was suggested to be realized using two enhancers per patterning gene: (i) a dynamic enhancer that encodes the wiring of the gene within the dynamic GRN, and (ii) a static enhancer that encodes the wiring of the gene within the static GRN (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This describes a key prediction of the Enhancer Switching model illustrated in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The gap gene Krüppel in Drosophila is regulated by two enhancers whose activities resemble those predicted by the Enhancer Switching model.
claims.source: The model is partially supported (or rather inspired) by observations in the early Drosophila embryo, where the gap gene Krüppel (Kr) was shown to be regulated by two enhancers whose activities resemble those predicted by the Enhancer Switching model (Zhu et al., 2017; El-Sherif and Levine, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing experimental evidence consistent with the model.

claims.claim: The Drosophila gap gene giant is regulated by enhancers with activities similar to those predicted by the Enhancer Switching model.
claims.source: Similar observations were made for the Drosophila gap gene giant (gt) (Hoermann et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claims.claim: In vertebrates, some enhancers or genetic programs mediate the initiation of segmentation clock waves posteriorly, while others mediate their anterior expression domains.
claims.source: Furthermore, in vertebrates, it has been suggested that some enhancers or genetic programs mediate the initiation of segmentation clock waves posteriorly, and others mediate their anterior expression domains (Oginuma et al., 2010; Shifley et al., 2008; Stauber et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on vertebrate segmentation.

claims.claim: Tribolium exhibits robust systemic RNAi, which facilitates the generation of RNAi knockdowns using parental RNAi.
claims.source: First, Tribolium exhibits robust systemic RNAi, which greatly eases the generation of RNAi knockdowns using parental RNAi (Bucher et al., 2002; Miller et al., 2012; Tomoyasu et al., 2008; Dönitz et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on Tribolium RNAi methods.

claims.claim: AP patterning in Tribolium takes place in the early embryo, which simplifies the interpretation of RNAi knockdowns generated using parental RNAi.
claims.source: Second, AP patterning takes place in the early Tribolium embryo, which eases the interpretation of RNAi knockdowns generated using parental RNAi, without the need for time-specific or tissue-specific genetic perturbations (Zhu et al., 2017; Boos et al., 2018; Choe and Brown, 2009; Bolognesi et al., 2008a; Choe et al., 2006; Kotkamp et al., 2010; Schoppmeier et al., 2009; Cerny et al., 2005; Bucher and Klingler, 2004; Schmitt-Engel et al., 2012; Marques-Souza et al., 2008; Savard et al., 2006; Marques-Souza, 2007; Jeon et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies on Tribolium development.

claims.claim: A wide array of genetic and genomic techniques has been developed for Tribolium.
claims.source: Third, a wide array of genetic and genomic techniques has been developed for Tribolium (Klingler and Bucher, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review of Tribolium methods.

claims.claim: ATAC-seq is fast and sensitive, requiring very little embryonic tissue compared to other open chromatin assays.
claims.source: In particular, 'Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin with high-throughput sequencing' (ATAC-seq) (Buenrostro et al., 2013) is fast and sensitive, and requires very little embryonic tissue (often one embryo, or even a tissue dissected from one embryo) compared to other open chromatin assays.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original ATAC-seq publication and represents established knowledge about the method.

claims.claim: Not all open chromatin regions are active enhancers; chromatin is also accessible at promoters, insulators, and regions bound by repressors.
claims.source: Nevertheless, not all open chromatin regions are active enhancers. Chromatin is also accessible at promoters, insulators, and regions bound by repressors (Thurman et al., 2012; Kok and Arnosti, 2015; Xi et al., 2007; Li and Arnosti, 2011), and hence, enhancer discovery using open chromatin assays has a high false positive rate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies on chromatin accessibility.

claims.claim: Chromatin accessibility is dynamic across space and time at active developmental enhancers compared to other regulatory elements like promoters.
claims.source: Interestingly, chromatin accessibility has been shown to be dynamic across space and time at active developmental enhancers compared to other regulatory elements like promoters (Reddington et al., 2020; Bozek et al., 2019; McKay and Lieb, 2013), and therefore, dynamic chromatin accessibility has been proposed as an accurate predictor for active enhancers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on chromatin dynamics.

claims.claim: This study used time-specific and tissue-specific ATAC-seq to elucidate the dynamics of open chromatin in space and time in early Tribolium embryos.
claims.source: Thus, in this paper, we used a time-specific and tissue-specific ATAC-seq assay to elucidate the dynamics of open chromatin in space and time in the early Tribolium embryos, used the assay to discover a number of active Tribolium enhancers, and assessed the association between differential ATAC-seq peak accessibility and enhancer activity.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological approach and primary finding of the current study.

claims.claim: Fluorescent proteins suffer from low degradation rates, which results in averaging out of fast-changing gene expression patterns.
claims.source: Nonetheless, FPs suffer from low degradation rates, which results in averaging out of fast-changing gene expression patterns, rendering them unsuitable for visualizing highly dynamic gene activities.
claims.evidence: This represents established knowledge about the limitations of fluorescent protein reporters.

claims.claim: MS2 tagging can be used to visualize de novo transcription, avoiding the averaging effect of using fluorescent proteins as reporters.
claims.source: This strategy can be used to visualize de novo transcription (El-Sherif and Levine, 2016; Lim et al., 2018; Garcia et al., 2013; Lucas et al., 2013; Bothma et al., 2014), avoiding the averaging effect of using FPs as reporters.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies using MS2 tagging.

claims.claim: This study established an MS2-tagging system in Tribolium to study the dynamics of gene expression waves during embryogenesis.
claims.source: Therefore, to study the dynamics of gene expression waves during embryogenesis, we established an MS2-tagging system in Tribolium, and used it to visualize the activities of some of the enhancers we discovered using our enhancer discovery system.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological achievement of the current study.

claims.claim: The study dissected Tribolium embryos at the germband stage into three regions (anterior, middle, and posterior) for ATAC-seq analysis.
claims.source: To that end, we dissected the Tribolium embryo at the germband stage into three regions across its AP axis (Figure 2A): anterior ('a'), middle ('m'), and posterior ('p'), and performed ATAC-seq on each region at two-time points: 23–26 hr after egg-lay (AEL) (hereafter, termed IT23), and 26–29 hr AEL (hereafter, termed IT26) (Materials and methods; see representative embryo from these two stages in Figure 2A').
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the ATAC-seq analysis, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: ATAC-seq libraries had an average of 1,835,762 unique, high-quality pairs of reads with 3.6X genomic coverage.
claims.source: ATAC-seq libraries compromised an average of 1,835,762 unique, high-quality pairs of reads (3.6 X genomic coverage, Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Biological replicates of ATAC-seq libraries were highly similar with a median Spearman's correlation coefficient of 0.875.
claims.source: Biological replicates of our ATAC-seq libraries were highly similar with a median Spearman's correlation coefficient of 0.875 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating the reproducibility of the data.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A total of 12,069 chromatin-accessible sites were identified in the ATAC-seq analysis.
claims.source: We identified a total of 12,069 chromatin-accessible sites (Materials and methods), with 4017 being specific to one or two particular regions of the germband and 1610 to a given time point (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: 46% of chromatin-accessible sites identified were intergenic or intronic.
claims.source: In agreement with the ability of ATAC-seq to detect distal regulatory elements in the genome (Buenrostro et al., 2013), a large proportion of these sites were intergenic or intronic (46%, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Principal component analysis of the most variable accessible sites mainly separated samples along the AP axis of the embryo.
claims.source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of most variable accessible sites (Materials and methods) mainly separated the samples along the AP axis of the embryo (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from PCA analysis shown in Figure 2B-D.

claims.claim: 3,106 chromatin-accessible sites (26% of the accessible genome) were differentially accessible when compared between different regions along the AP axis and/or time point.
claims.source: Among all 12,069 sites, 3106 (26% of the accessible genome) were differentially accessible when compared between different regions along the AP axis and/or time point (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from differential accessibility analysis.

claims.claim: 62% of constitutively accessible sites corresponded to promoters and gene bodies.
claims.source: Remarkably, while 62% of the constitutively accessible sites corresponded to promoters and gene bodies, 66% of the differentially accessible sites were intergenic or intronic, and this proportion was even higher (74%) among the differentially accessible sites with more specific patterns of accessibility (Figure 2E), suggesting that spatiotemporal control of transcription in the early Tribolium embryo is largely mediated by enhancers as opposed to promoters.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: 66% of differentially accessible sites were intergenic or intronic.

claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Spatiotemporal control of transcription in the early Tribolium embryo is largely mediated by enhancers as opposed to promoters.
claims.source: Remarkably, while 62% of the constitutively accessible sites corresponded to promoters and gene bodies, 66% of the differentially accessible sites were intergenic or intronic, and this proportion was even higher (74%) among the differentially accessible sites with more specific patterns of accessibility (Figure 2E), suggesting that spatiotemporal control of transcription in the early Tribolium embryo is largely mediated by enhancers as opposed to promoters.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential distribution of accessible sites shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: 2,109 sites were differentially accessible along the AP axis at a particular time point, with the majority along the AP axis at IT26.
claims.source: When comparing accessibility along the AP axis at a particular time point, 2109 sites were differentially accessible, the majority of them along the AP axis at IT26.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from differential accessibility analysis.

claims.claim: Only 132 sites were differentially accessible between IT26 and IT23 at the same portion of the embryo.
claims.source: In addition, only 132 sites were differentially accessible between IT26 and IT23 at the same portion of the embryo (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from differential accessibility analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C.

claims.claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility in Tribolium at the developmental stages studied are primarily associated with space rather than time.
claims.source: Together, our findings indicate that changes in chromatin accessibility in Tribolium at this developmental stage are primarily associated with space rather than time, and are particularly evident when comparing the anterior part of the germband to the middle and posterior parts.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential accessibility analysis results.

claims.claim: Dynamically accessible sites are especially likely to be associated with enhancer activity.
claims.source: Furthermore, our data are in line with observations made by other authors (Cusanovich et al., 2018; Bozek and Gompel, 2020) that suggests that dynamically accessible sites are especially likely to be associated with enhancer activity, laying the foundation for a promising enhancer prediction strategy based on differential ATAC-seq peak analysis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to other studies and the current study's data.

claims.claim: An enhancer reporter system has been previously established in Tribolium using mCherry as a reporter gene.
claims.source: An enhancer reporter system has been previously established in Tribolium using mCherry as a reporter gene (Lai et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Long half-lives of mCherry mRNA and proteins could average out fast transcriptional dynamics.
claims.source: However, long half-lives of mCherry mRNA and proteins could average out fast transcriptional dynamics, precluding the analysis of gene expression waves.
claims.evidence: This represents established knowledge about the limitations of mCherry as a reporter.

claims.claim: The study created a Tribolium enhancer reporter system capable of visualizing de novo transcription in both fixed and live embryos.
claims.source: To circumvent this, we created a Tribolium enhancer reporter system capable of visualizing de novo transcription in both fixed and live embryos.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological achievement of the current study.

claims.claim: The enhancer reporter system uses the gene yellow, which has a long intron (2.7 kb).
claims.source: Our enhancer reporter system is composed of the gene yellow, which has a long intron (2.7 kb).
claims.evidence: This describes a component of the reporter system developed in the study.

claims.claim: Visualizing intronic transcription of the reporter gene yellow using in situ staining enables the detection of de novo transcription.
claims.source: Visualizing intronic transcription of the reporter gene yellow using in situ staining in fixed embryos enables the detection of de novo transcription, and has been routinely used to analyze fast transcriptional dynamics in enhancer reporter experiments in Drosophila (Perry et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published method and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: The study successfully generated a transgenic beetle line carrying the MCP-mEmerald construct with ubiquitous mEmerald fluorescence.
claims.source: Via piggyBac transgenesis, we successfully generated a transgenic beetle line carrying the MCP-mEmerald construct, in which a ubiquitous mEmerald fluorescence is detected (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This describes an experimental achievement shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The study successfully generated a transgenic beetle line carrying the hbA >MS2-yellow construct.
claims.source: Via piggyBac transgenesis, we successfully generated a transgenic beetle line carrying the hbA >MS2-yellow construct.
claims.evidence: This describes an experimental achievement of the study.

claims.claim: Yellow expression in the hbA >MS2-yellow line is similar to mCherry expression in a previously tested hbA >mCherry line.
claims.source: Examining yellow expression using in situ hybridization chain reaction (HCR) (Choi et al., 2018) in early hbA >MS2-yellow embryos using both exonic (Figure 3E and F) and intronic (Figure 3F) probes, we confirmed that the yellow expression in hbA >MS2-yellow line is similar to the mCherry expression in a previously tested hbA >mCherry line (Lai et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results from the current study (Figure 3E and F) with a previous study (Lai et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Bright mEmerald puncta in hbA >MS2-yellow; aTub >MCP-mEmerald embryos are distributed along the AP axis initially as a cap that eventually refines into a stripe.
claims.source: Imaging early embryos of the progeny (hbA >MS2-yellow; aTub >MCP-mEmerald) (Video 1; Figure 3G), we observed weak and diffuse mEmerald signal within the nuclei, and bright puncta at a rate of at most one punctum per nucleus. The bright mEmerald puncta are distributed along the AP axis initially as a cap that eventually refines into a stripe (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), resembling the yellow expression of the hbA enhancer reporter visualized using in situ HCR staining (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from live imaging experiments shown in Video 1, Figure 3G, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Bright mEmerald puncta in hbA >MS2-yellow; aTub >MCP-mEmerald embryos are mEmerald enrichments at transcribed MS2 loops, reflecting de novo transcription driven by the hbA enhancer.
claims.source: We conclude, therefore, that such bright mEmerald puncta are mEmerald enrichments at transcribed MS2 loops, reflecting the de novo transcription driven by the hbA enhancer.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the live imaging observations and comparison with in situ staining.

claims.claim: The MS2-MCP enhancer reporter system is capable of visualizing enhancer activity in live Tribolium embryos.
claims.source: Hence, both individual nuclei of the early Tribolium embryo and de novo transcription driven by the hbA enhancer can be visualized and detected in a single cross of hbA >MS2-yellow line and the MCP-mEmerald line, confirming our success in establishing an MS2-MCP enhancer reporter system that is capable of visualizing enhancer activity in live Tribolium embryos.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results demonstrating the functionality of the system.

claims.claim: Out of nine tested enhancer reporters, four successfully drove yellow expression in the early Tribolium embryo.

claims.claim: Enhancer hbB drove an expression that overlaps with hb expression in the serosa.

claims.claim: Out of six active enhancer constructs, five (83%) overlapped differentially accessible sites.
claims.source: We found that out of the six active constructs, five (83%) overlapped differentially accessible sites, while one (17%) overlapped a site that was not differentially accessible.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of the association between differential accessibility and enhancer activity.

claims.claim: Out of five non-active enhancer constructs, three (60%) overlapped sites that were differentially accessible.
claims.source: In contrast, out of the five non-active constructs, three (60%) overlapped sites that were differentially accessible, while the remaining two (40%) overlapped sites that were not differentially accessible (Figure 4D; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for details).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: About 60% of analyzed differentially accessible sites were associated with active enhancers.
claims.source: Therefore, about 60% of analyzed differentially accessible sites were associated with active enhancers whereas only 30% of analyzed constitutively accessible sites were associated with active enhancer regions (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Only 30% of analyzed constitutively accessible sites were associated with active enhancer regions.
claims.source: Therefore, about 60% of analyzed differentially accessible sites were associated with active enhancers whereas only 30% of analyzed constitutively accessible sites were associated with active enhancer regions (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The trend in the data is in line with observations in other model systems suggesting that differential accessibility is associated with enhancer activity.
claims.source: Although the sample size is small, the trend is in line with observations in other model systems (Cusanovich et al., 2018; Bozek and Gompel, 2020) suggesting that differential accessibility is associated with enhancer activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's data and comparison with cited studies.

claims.claim: The Enhancer Switching model predicts that expression patterns driven by dynamic enhancers progressively decrease in the posterior-to-anterior direction.
claims.source: Carefully analyzing model outputs for the total activity of constituent genes, static enhancer reporters, and dynamic enhancer reporters revealed two characteristics of the spatiotemporal dynamics of their activities (Figure 5A). First, endogenous genes and reporters of their dynamic and static enhancers are all expressed in waves that propagate from posterior to anterior (Figure 5A). Second, expression patterns driven by dynamic enhancers progressively decrease in the posterior-to-anterior direction, matching the progressive decrease of the speed regulator concentration (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from computational simulations of the model shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The Enhancer Switching model predicts that expression patterns driven by static enhancers progressively increase in the posterior-to-anterior direction.
claims.source: On the other hand, expression patterns driven by static enhancers progressively increase in the posterior-to-anterior direction, opposite to the direction of the increase of the speed regulator concentration (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from computational simulations of the model shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Endogenous run expression periodically arises from the posterior and gradually propagates towards the anterior, forming a stable striped expression.
claims.source: Endogenous run expression (green in Figure 6A) periodically arises from the posterior and gradually propagates towards the anterior, forming a stable striped expression (that eventually fades).

claims.claim: The expression wave of runB >yellow appears weakly in the posterior and gradually strengthens as it propagates towards anterior.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.source: Second, runB activity progressively increases in the posterior-to-anterior direction, corresponding inversely with the progressive drop of concentration of the Caudal (Cad) gradient (Figure 6B), which has been suggested to act as a speed regulator for pair-rule and gap genes in Tribolium (El-Sherif et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2017), and more generally, an evolutionary conserved posterior determinant in arthropods (along with Wnt) (Auman et al., 2017; Bolognesi et al., 2008a; Schönauer et al., 2016; Bolognesi et al., 2008b; Copf et al., 2004; McGregor et al., 2008; Novikova et al., 2020; Miyawaki et al., 2004).

claims.claim: The degradation delay of the reporter gene yellow is larger than that of endogenous run, leading to averaging out of run expression wave dynamics.
claims.source: This shows that, indeed, the degradation delay of the reporter gene yellow is larger than that of an endogenous run, leading to averaging out of run expression wave dynamics, a problem that can be alleviated using intronic in situ staining.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing exonic and intronic in situ staining results.

claims.claim: runB drives a wave of activity that progressively increases in strength as it propagates from posterior to anterior.
claims.source: Tracking the accumulated activity in space, after discounting nuclear/cellular flow, revealed that runB indeed drives a wave of activity that progressively increase in strength as it propagates from posterior to anterior (Video 6; Figure 6D), fitting the role of a 'static enhancer' within our Enhancer Switching model.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from live imaging analysis shown in Video 6 and Figure 6D.

claims.claim: runB activity dynamics are consistent with the role of a static enhancer within the Enhancer Switching model.
claims.source: Tracking the accumulated activity in space, after discounting nuclear/cellular flow, revealed that runB indeed drives a wave of activity that progressively increase in strength as it propagates from posterior to anterior (Video 6; Figure 6D), fitting the role of a 'static enhancer' within our Enhancer Switching model. However, this merely shows that runB activity dynamics are consistent with our model, but is still far from strongly supporting the model (more on that in the Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing live imaging observations with model predictions.

claims.claim: Enhancer hbA drives a wave of activity that propagates from posterior to anterior.
claims.source: We found that enhancer hbA drives a wave of activity that propagates from posterior to anterior (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from live imaging analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Enhancer hbA drives strong expression in the posterior that weakens as it propagates towards the anterior.
claims.source: In contrast to enhancer runB, however, we found that enhancer hbA drives strong expression in the posterior that weakens as it propagates towards the anterior (compare Figure 6D and E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from live imaging analysis shown in Figure 6D and E.

claims.claim: hbA either drives the entirety of hb expression or acts as a dynamic enhancer within the Enhancer Switching model.
claims.source: As concluded by our simulations of the Enhancer Switching model (Figure 5B), this indicates that hbA either drives the entirety of hb expression, or acts as a dynamic enhancer within the Enhancer Switching model.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing live imaging observations with model predictions shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Strong support for the Enhancer Switching model requires finding enhancer pairs for several gap and pair-rule genes whose activity dynamics match those predicted for static and dynamic enhancers.
claims.source: We present these findings as tentative support for the Enhancer Switching model, whereas a strong support requires: (Spitz and Furlong, 2012) finding enhancer pairs for several gap and pair-rule genes whose activity dynamics match those predicted for static and dynamic enhancers, and (Shlyueva et al., 2014) verifying that the deletion of either dynamic or static enhancers result in phenotypes predicted by the model (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This outlines the criteria for strong support of the model, representing the authors' assessment of what evidence is needed.

claims.claim: Strong support for the Enhancer Switching model requires verifying that the deletion of either dynamic or static enhancers results in phenotypes predicted by the model.
claims.source: We present these findings as tentative support for the Enhancer Switching model, whereas a strong support requires: (Spitz and Furlong, 2012) finding enhancer pairs for several gap and pair-rule genes whose activity dynamics match those predicted for static and dynamic enhancers, and (Shlyueva et al., 2014) verifying that the deletion of either dynamic or static enhancers result in phenotypes predicted by the model (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This outlines the criteria for strong support of the model, representing the authors' assessment of what evidence is needed.

claims.claim: Deleting a static enhancer should reduce the gene expression wave into an almost homogenously oscillating or sequentially activating domain at the posterior that fails to resolve into gene expression bands anteriorly.
claims.source: Specifically, deleting a static enhancer should reduce the gene expression wave into an (almost) homogenously oscillating (or sequentially activating) domain at the posterior, that fails to resolve into gene expression bands anteriorly (Figure 7B), while deleting a dynamic enhancer should abolish the entire gene expression (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the Enhancer Switching model illustrated in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Deleting a dynamic enhancer should abolish the entire gene expression.
claims.source: Specifically, deleting a static enhancer should reduce the gene expression wave into an (almost) homogenously oscillating (or sequentially activating) domain at the posterior, that fails to resolve into gene expression bands anteriorly (Figure 7B), while deleting a dynamic enhancer should abolish the entire gene expression (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the Enhancer Switching model illustrated in Figure 7C.

results.result: Gene expression patterns in vertebrates and short-germ insects like Tribolium show dynamic, wavelike patterns rather than the stable domains observed in Drosophila, but the enhancer-level mechanisms mediating these waves are unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 establish the scientific context and motivation for the study. The claims are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (C3, C4, C11-C14) and represent accepted knowledge in the field. The identification of a knowledge gap (C5) is appropriate and justified.

results.result: The study established an ATAC-seq-based enhancer prediction system in Tribolium using spatially and temporally resolved chromatin accessibility profiling, identifying 12,069 accessible sites with changes primarily associated with spatial rather than temporal differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C32, C35-C42, C47-C49 describe the ATAC-seq methodology and results with specific quantitative data (e.g., 12,069 sites, 0.875 correlation, 3.6X coverage). The experimental design is clearly described, replicates show high correlation, and the conclusion about spatial vs temporal dynamics is supported by the differential accessibility analysis. This is a well-executed technical achievement.

results.result: Differentially accessible chromatin sites are enriched for intergenic and intronic regions (66-74%) compared to constitutively accessible sites (38%), suggesting that spatiotemporal transcriptional control in Tribolium is largely mediated by enhancers rather than promoters.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 provide specific quantitative data showing the genomic distribution of accessible sites. The inference that enhancers mediate spatiotemporal control (C46) is reasonable given the enrichment of differential accessibility in intergenic/intronic regions. Claim C50 appropriately contextualizes this with citations to similar findings in other systems.

results.result: The study successfully established an MS2-MCP enhancer reporter system in Tribolium capable of visualizing de novo transcription in both fixed and live embryos, validated using the hbA enhancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C61 describe the development and validation of the MS2-MCP system with clear experimental evidence. The system was successfully implemented (C56, C57), validated against previous results (C58), and shown to detect transcription sites as bright puncta (C59, C60). This represents a significant technical achievement with appropriate controls and validation.

results.result: Using the enhancer prediction and reporter systems, the study discovered and validated several Tribolium enhancers, with 4 out of 9 tested enhancers (hbA, hbB, runA, runB) successfully driving yellow expression in patterns overlapping endogenous gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C62-C66 report the discovery and validation of enhancers with specific quantitative results (4/9 active). The expression patterns driven by each enhancer are described and compared to endogenous expression, providing clear experimental validation of enhancer activity.

results.result: Differential chromatin accessibility is associated with enhancer activity: 83% (5/6) of active enhancer constructs overlapped differentially accessible sites, while only 60% of differentially accessible sites were associated with active enhancers compared to 30% of constitutively accessible sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 present quantitative data on the association between differential accessibility and enhancer activity. However, the sample size is explicitly acknowledged as small (C71), and the predictive value is modest (60% vs 30%). While the trend supports the hypothesis, the limited sample size and moderate enrichment make this result suggestive rather than conclusive. Additional validation with more enhancers would strengthen this finding.

results.result: The Speed Regulation and Enhancer Switching models propose that gene expression waves are generated through a morphogen gradient modulating the balance between dynamic and static gene regulatory networks, with each gene regulated by separate dynamic and static enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C22 describe theoretical models previously proposed by some authors, supported by computational simulations (C17, C18) and prior experimental evidence in Tribolium (C19). These claims accurately represent the models and their prior support, though they are primarily theoretical frameworks rather than new experimental findings in this study.

results.result: The Enhancer Switching model predicts that dynamic enhancers drive expression that decreases in the posterior-to-anterior direction, while static enhancers drive expression that increases in the posterior-to-anterior direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 describe specific predictions from computational simulations of the Enhancer Switching model shown in Figure 5A. These predictions are clearly derived from the model and provide testable hypotheses for experimental validation.

results.result: Enhancer runB drives periodic waves that propagate posterior-to-anterior with progressively increasing strength, inversely correlating with the Caudal gradient, consistent with the predicted behavior of a static enhancer in the Enhancer Switching model.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77, C80-C82 present experimental observations from in situ staining and live imaging showing that runB activity increases anterior-ward, opposite to the Caudal gradient. The data are consistent with model predictions (C82), though the authors appropriately note this is consistency rather than strong support. The intronic staining control (C80) addresses a technical limitation.

results.result: Enhancer hbA drives a wave that propagates posterior-to-anterior with strong posterior expression that weakens anteriorly, indicating it either drives the entirety of hb expression or acts as a dynamic enhancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 present live imaging observations of hbA activity. The interpretation (C85) appropriately acknowledges ambiguity: the observed pattern is consistent with either a dynamic enhancer or an enhancer driving total gene expression. This honest assessment of interpretive limitations is appropriate given the data.

results.result: The data are consistent with the Enhancer Switching model in which dynamic and static enhancers balance to control gene expression timing, but strong support requires finding enhancer pairs for multiple genes and validating predicted deletion phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C86-C89 present the main interpretive conclusion and explicitly acknowledge its limitations. The authors appropriately state the data are 'consistent with' rather than 'prove' the model (C9, C82), identify what additional evidence is needed (C86-C87), and make specific testable predictions (C88-C89). This represents appropriate scientific caution and transparency about the strength of support for the model.

results.result: Previous studies in Drosophila and vertebrates have identified enhancers with activities resembling those predicted by the Enhancer Switching model.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 cite prior work showing evidence consistent with the Enhancer Switching model in other organisms. These claims appropriately contextualize the current study within existing literature and are supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: Tribolium is well-suited for studying dynamic gene expression due to its robust RNAi, early AP patterning, available genetic tools, and the advantages and limitations of ATAC-seq and MS2 tagging are well-established.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C34, C51-C52 describe established knowledge about Tribolium as a model system and the technical methods used. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to published literature and represent accurate characterizations of established techniques and their properties.

results.result: Gene expression waves during embryonic patterning have been documented in vertebrates, Tribolium, and even Drosophila, with Caudal/Wnt acting as conserved posterior determinants in arthropods.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14, C78-C79 cite extensive prior literature documenting gene expression waves across multiple model systems and the role of Caudal/Wnt. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations and represent established knowledge that contextualizes the current study.
